n: Elijah appears without introduction and confronts Ahab with a drought. His name means “my God is Jehovah”—a direct challenge to Baal, the supposed rain-god. Latter-day Saints honor Elijah as holding the sealing power, by which his word could bind the heavens.

f.g: Hebrew Eliyahu: ‘my God is Jehovah (the LORD).’
from Tishbe, a town in Gilead east of the Jordan.
whom I serve, as a servant stands ready before a king.

n: Immediately after Elijah’s declaration, the Lord gives him new direction.
He is sent into hiding east toward the Jordan, by a stream called Cherith—out of Ahab’s reach.

f.g: a seasonal stream (wadi), probably east of the Jordan; location uncertain.
east of, or facing, the Jordan.

n: God promises water from the brook and food from ravens—unclean birds under the law, now serving as God’s messengers of provision.

f.g: unclean birds under the law of Moses.

n: Elijah obeys exactly. His public boldness is matched by private trust and obedience.
Morning and evening the ravens bring bread and meat, recalling the manna and quail God gave Israel in the wilderness.

f.w: bread and flesh in the morning

n: Eventually the brook dries up. Elijah experiences the drought he announced, and must trust God for the next step.
Once again, the Lord’s word comes when needed.
God sends him to Zarephath, a Phoenician town near Sidon—Jezebel’s home territory and the heartland of Baal worship. There a widow, one of society’s poorest, will feed him.

f.g: a coastal town between Tyre and Sidon; in Greek, Sarepta.

n: At the town gate he meets a widow gathering sticks and asks for water—a precious thing in a drought.
As she goes, he also asks for a piece of bread, a far harder request.
She swears by “the LORD thy God,” recognizing Elijah as an Israelite. She has only enough flour and oil for one last meal before she and her son starve.
Elijah tells her not to fear, but to feed him first. It is a test of faith: give from her little before seeing the miracle.
He gives the Lord’s promise: her flour and oil will last until rain returns. Israel’s God provides in the land of Baal.
She obeys, and she, her son, and Elijah eat for many days.
The miracle continues day after day, exactly as promised. Many see it as a type of how the Lord blesses those who give in faith, as with the widow’s mite.

f.w: the barrel of meal wasted not

n: Later, her son becomes so ill that he stops breathing and dies.
In grief, she assumes that the presence of a holy man has exposed some past sin and brought punishment. Her question reflects a common ancient belief that suffering always comes from sin.

f.w: What have I to do with thee
f.g: an idiom meaning ‘Why are you involved with me?’ or ‘What have you against me?’

n: Elijah takes the boy from her arms to his upper room and lays him on his own bed.

f.g: an upper room or roof chamber.

n: Elijah pours out his heart honestly to God, asking why such sorrow should fall on the woman who had sheltered him.
He stretches himself on the child three times and pleads for the boy’s life to return. This is the first recorded raising of the dead in the Bible.

f.g: Hebrew nephesh: life, breath, living being.

n: The Lord hears Elijah, and the boy comes back to life. God holds power over death itself—a foreshadowing of Christ’s raising of the widow’s son at Nain and His own resurrection.
Elijah brings the boy down and gives him back to his mother with simple words: “See, your son lives.”
The widow’s faith becomes certainty: Elijah is truly God’s prophet, and the Lord’s word through him is true. A Gentile woman confesses the God of Israel, while Israel itself serves Baal.
